patient_information: A 24-year-old Dutch yoga instructor who has been a strict vegan for the past 8 years. She has no known immunosuppression.
chief_complaint: An episode of strange sensations in the right side of the body.
history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with an episode of 'pins and needles' sensations that started in the right side of her face, marched to her right arm, and then involved her right leg, lasting for about 2 minutes. This was described as a focal epileptic seizure, a Jacksonian 'sensory march'. She had experienced a similar episode several months prior but did not seek medical attention at that time.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Four years prior to presentation, the patient left The Netherlands for a 2-year backpacking trip. She travelled extensively through South America (Ecuador, Peru, Argentina) and South-east Asia (Thailand, Laos, Cambodia), staying in hostels, private accommodations, and with local people in the countryside. As a vegan, her main diet consisted of fruits, vegetables, nuts, and rice from local vendors, but never any animal products.
vitals: The patient was afebrile on examination.
physical_exam: On examination, the patient looked well. Her neurological examination was completely unremarkable, and the rest of her physical examination was also normal.
labs_and_diagnostics: Routine blood investigations, including a differential blood count and C-reactive protein, were completely normal. A CSF examination was also unremarkable. An MRI of the brain with gadolinium enhancement revealed multiple cortical and subcortical cystic lesions in both hemispheres, with some lesions showing perifocal oedema and ring-enhancement. An enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) for anticysticercal antibodies was positive in both serum and CSF.
differential_diagnosis: The diagnosis was primarily guided by the combination of the clinical presentation (focal seizure in a healthy-looking, afebrile patient), extensive travel history to endemic regions in South America and South-east Asia, and classic neuroimaging findings. The multiple cystic lesions on MRI strongly suggested neurocysticercosis, which was subsequently confirmed with serology.
management_and_clinical_course: The patient was treated with albendazole 400mg twice daily for 10 days and was started on antiepileptic drugs. She declined treatment with corticosteroids. She remained seizure-free, and a follow-up MRI one year later showed regression of all cysts. A CT scan at the two-year follow-up revealed two calcifications. Her antiepileptic medication was stopped after she remained seizure-free for a period of 3 years.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was neurocysticercosis, an infection of the central nervous system with the larval form of Taenia solium. The diagnosis was established based on the clinical presentation of a focal seizure, a history of extensive travel in endemic regions, and characteristic MRI findings of multiple cystic brain lesions. The diagnosis was confirmed by a positive enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) for anticysticercal antibodies in both serum and CSF.
